articles.title: Chain reaction that begins when tumor suppression gene is switched off offers clues to how cancer develops
articles.description: A tumor suppressor gene known as p53 is mutated in more than half of all cancers, but how it acts to prevent cancer formation is largely unknown. A study by UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers sheds light on this phenomenon by showing what happens when p53 becomes disabled, revealing the gene's diverse roles in maintaining healthy metabolic activity, repressing mobile genes called retrotransposons and preventing cells from adopting features of sperm and eggs.

This system has been shown to remain stable for more than 24 hours without intervention, and the related findings are published in the journal Nature.

articles.title: A revisit of World War II through labor and civil rights at Red Emma's Bookstore
articles.description: On Thursday, Oct. 1, Cornell Assistant Professor of History Tejasvi Nagaraja presented his new book at Red Emma's in a conversation with Hopkins Associate Professor of History and Director of the Chloe Center Stuart Schrader . The event featured Nagaraja's Troop Movements: Labor, Race, and Global Freedom Struggles in America's World War II . The book adopts a bottom-up, multi-scalar approach, examining how World War II mobilization brought workers into overlapping struggles over labor, race, citizenship and broader political and societal change during and after the war. Schrader opened the conversation by emphasizing the book's attention to ordinary people's ability to shape political change. "World War II is thought of as a moment of political consensus, but when you look beneath the surface, there was a lot of contestation and conflict, [...] and a lot of that conflict was powered by workers who were trying to build more equal and racially integrated workplaces," Schrader commented. Nagaraja teaches at Cornell's School of Industrial and Labor Relations. He began his presentation with photographs of actors and activists Ossie Davis and Ruby Dee. By drawing connections between their wartime experiences and their later activism, Nagaraja argued that World War II should not be understood solely as a period of national unity against Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan. Instead, Nagaraja centered defence workers and military personnel who participated in strikes, civil-rights campaigns and protests over working conditions and racial discrimination while contributing to the war effort. "World War II is not just this nice prologue of unity." Nagaraja said, "Actually, the conflicts that happened in the early 1940s tell us a lot about the conflicts that would shape the 60s and the 2020s." Schrader then asked why Nagaraja places defense-industry workers and soldiers within the same framework. "The lines were blurred between the foreign and the domestic in this particular war," said Nagaraja, "tens of millions were serving in the armed forces and the defense industries in what I call a composite workforce, and that created blurred experiences and the possibilities for linked coalitions too." Nagaraja also connected wartime racial politics to policing. He recounted the 1942 killing of Black servicemember Thomas Broadus by a Baltimore police officer while Broadus was on leave. The case became a rallying point for local civil-rights activists, labor organizers and students, who organized around demands such as police reform, housing rights and desegregation. The conversation later widened beyond Baltimore to the immediate aftermath of the war. Nagaraja described 1945 and 1946 as an uncertain period between World War II and the emerging Cold War, when workers and service members across different countries organized strikes and protests while anti-colonial movements challenged European empires. He pointed to American service members and merchant mariners who questioned support for European efforts to restore colonial control in places such as Vietnam and Indonesia. "They actually made people-to-people connections in that moment," Nagaraja said, "and they envisioned another world." Returning to the civil rights movement, Schrader asked how the organizing of the 1940s connected to the activism of the 1960s. Nagaraja pointed to wartime migration and military service as opportunities for Black workers to build coalitions across regions and national borders. "And so that civil rights movement was a labor movement, and that civil rights movement was in tension with policing and incarceration, and that civil rights movement was a global struggle," Nagaraja said. Eva Klaus, a student at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, recalled how the event offered an opportunity to explore activism and meet people with shared interests in an interview with The News-Letter . "This is one of the events that I liked the most." Klaus continued, "I actually read part of his book while he was doing the talk, and while of course it's difficult to both absorb the information that I read and listen to his talk, I really liked the amount of depth he went into with his not only his book but his actual talks." Baltimore resident Ryan Hardey, who works on global trade policy, said his interest came from the relationship between war and social movements in an interview with The News-Letter . "Being present in a longer conversation with somebody, especially like Tej, who's such an expert," Hardey stated. "It just makes us smarter people."

articles.title: Oculi and its quest to see the world
articles.description: From Shinkansen bullet trains to suits for swimming , nature has always been an engineer's greatest source of inspiration. Now, researchers are turning to the human eye as they look to accelerate physical AI , the branch of artificial intelligence that lets machines interact with and adapt to the physical world. In an interview with The News-Letter , Charbel Rizk , a former professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the Whiting School of Engineering, shared the work that his startup , Oculi , is doing in this field. Rizk, who hails from Jezzine, a mountainous town in Lebanon (a country he emphasized is, in fact, not a desert), became interested in autonomous vehicles while pursuing his PhD at Georgia Tech . "[I participated in] a competition for autonomous drones to fly from point A to point B, pick up an object, deliver it to point C and come back to point A." His team became the first to conceptualize and build a quadcopter . This four-rotor design is very stable because two rotors spin clockwise and the other two spin counterclockwise, generating equal and opposite torques that keep it in the air. Rizk recounted demonstrating the design to a U.S. Navy captain, an encounter which suggested people can often not see immediate value in ingenious ideas. "[The captain] looked at it and said 'That's a pretty cool toy, but what do I do with it?'" However, they could only afford to carry one camera on board, given the bulky size of the computer that processed video in real time to aid in navigation. "That's really when I realized that the world of AI, the world of autonomy, is not going to take off unless you solve the vision problem." Rizk said, alluding to his eureka moment. Rizk corroborated the hypothesis that vision was the limiting factor in translating many technologies into real-world products while working in the aerospace industry and collaborating with the defense world, settings in which people still relied on the traditional camera and computer set-up to collect data and make decisions in real time. Inspired by the human eye's ability to process visual information alongside the brain, detecting contrast, color and minute details, Rizk founded Oculi. Its technology centers on the sensing and processing unit (SPU) it created. The SPU is composed of pixels with individual logic and memory, allowing each pixel to process the visual data it captures and determine whether it is of interest before sending it to a downstream processing unit. This approach can minimize energy consumption by reducing the power required for data transfer. Additionally, Oculi offers an enticing solution for data privacy, as its technology can make decisions without even generating an image of the scene. However, a trade-off remains between collecting more data - on the off-chance it is needed - and giving up data that might be useful. "You can save up to $50 billion in energy every year if you make them smart," Rizk described. Oculi's main focus is commercial applications of its SPU. Take sliding doors, for instance. Rizk believes that instead of going after superintelligence , current work in the field should stop and consider basic functions in the world that still aren't well automated, like why a sliding door opens even when walking past it or just waving a hand in front of it. With Oculi's SPU, this issue could be tackled by programming the door to open only when someone walks toward it with the intention of passing through. Rizk explained these applications might not have the same allure as using an SPU in unmanned defense vehicles operating in off-grid terrain, but they could have an immediate impact. In Northern Japan, for example, black bears sometimes venture into urban environments in winter to find food. There have been instances where bears have gone into supermarkets simply because a sliding door opened for them, a calamity that could easily have been avoided with an SPU. Adding vision can also reduce pedestrian deaths, help the visually impaired community and cut energy and money wasted on heating, cooling and lighting. Rizk is fueled by problems like these, which exemplify what it means to engineer solutions for humanity's greater good. He is quick to point out, however, that in startups - unlike in academia - he has to consider not just what he wants to do, but also what his investors want. When asked what advice he would give students grappling with different career options, he was clear: be honest with yourself and ask whether you're competent and self-motivated. "[If you are,] you should go start your own company or join a startup or small company," Rizk remarked. The future for physical AI is promising, particularly as startups like Oculi pave the way for dynamic solutions that can revolutionize everything from traffic management systems to electronic devices. Rizk firmly believes the vision problem is the Achilles' heel we need to tackle to engineer a safer, greener and more efficient future.

articles.title: MLB playoffs: takeaways from the Wild Card
articles.description: The Wild Card Round of the MLB playoffs is now complete, with the Braves, Padres, White Sox and Yankees punching their way into the Divisional Round. Only one series went the distance, as the Braves and Phillies continued their semi-annual battle in a winner-take-all game three, while each of the other series ended in clean 2-0 sweeps. Eight teams now remain, vying for the World Series, and here are my takeaways from the Wild Card Round as well as what I am looking forward to in these upcoming series. "Chris Sale and Pray for Hail" I am a Braves fan and couldn't resist writing about the Braves finally getting over the hump in the postseason against their always feisty division rival. The Phillies have been death for America's Team in the past decade but clutch hitting and unlikely big-time performances on the mound proved to be enough for the Braves to outlast the Phillies in 2026. In the '50s, there was a catchphrase of "Spahn then Sain then pray for rain" when the Braves only had two good starting pitchers, but for the 2026 Braves, "Chris Sale and Pray for Hail" might be more accurate. Injuries have hampered the Braves' rotation, requiring Chris Sale to put the team on his back in this three-game set, pitching into the seventh inning in the Game 1 victory before getting the final four outs in Game 3 on only one day's rest. Journeyman Ray Kerr also had a huge performance in the deciding game of the series, but a beleaguered Braves team now stares down a Goliath in the Los Angeles Dodgers in the Divisional Round. Don't cross your fingers. A Yankees three-Headed monster Maddux, Glavine and Smoltz. Schlittler, Fried and Cole. That could very well be the company for this trio of starters atop the Yankees rotation. Fried and Cole are well-established veterans who have been torturing big league hitters for a decade, while 25-year-old Cam Schlittler has burst onto the scene in his first full MLB season with a Cy Young-caliber season. The three are also already more than proven when October rolls around. Max Fried was part of the 2021 Braves World Series squad, while Gerrit Cole has pitched in two different World Series and owns a 2.77 ERA in 133.1 career postseason innings. Cam Schlitter has the shortest resume of the three but in his young career has been an outstanding big game performer. In his three career postseason appearances, he has only allowed two runs in 20.2 innings. The Rays earned the top spot in the American League, but the Yankees have firepower in their rotation that perhaps only New York money can buy. This series will be the classic clash between a scrappy small market team and the bruising Bronx Bombers roster. Is anyone hotter than the Padres? The San Diego Padres finished the season scorching hot and parlayed that into a decisive sweep of the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card. Their success is in large part due to a plethora of backend bullpen arms highlighted by star closer Mason Miller. Miller has been unhittable this year. He sports a 1.67 ERA while leading the NL in saves and recording 129 strikeouts in only 70 innings. Adrian Morejon, Bradgley Rodriguez and Yuki Matsui have also been dominant in 2026, giving the Padres an arsenal of relief pitchers at their disposal. Their lineup also packs some punch with star outfielder Fernando Tatis Jr. leading the charge. The Friars match up with the Milwaukee Brewers in the Divisional Round and will be heavy underdogs. However, history has shown that momentum and a bullpen can get you a long way in the MLB playoffs, so watch out for the Padres to potentially go on a run.

articles.title: Inside the Longchamp, unpacked
articles.description: I can't go a single day at Homewood without seeing someone carrying the Longchamp and Owala combo, and unfortunately I am one of them. The contents of my bag are probably also pretty typical, but it's not the items themselves that make my bag personal; it's the stories attached to them. 1. The bag itself : This navy Longchamp Le Pliage Original Tote bag has been around longer than I have, always faithfully draped over my mom's shoulder on every errand, vacation and doctor's appointment. Using that very bag now for college feels almost surreal; I spent my childhood watching it follow my mom through so much of her adult life, and now it follows me as I begin mine. The frayed corners and the worn leather straps make me feel as though she's right here with me. Carrying my mom's bag each day has become a way of keeping her close while she's more than 3,000 miles away. 2. HeyTea laptop sleeve : I never used a laptop sleeve before, but apparently all it took was a free one to change that. Over the summer, my best friend and I woke up at six in the morning and drove 30 minutes to the grand opening of the HeyTea in my hometown. The result? This free white puffy laptop sleeve, which now houses my Mac. 3. My iPad : a non-negotiable for notes and schoolwork. My 30-hour GoodNotes screen time each week can probably speak for itself. 4. My Owala : an investment made by my 10th-grade self. The scratches and dents are evidence of all the highs and lows we've been through together. It's become my emotional support water bottle, even though it's gotten a little wobbly on its feet after all these years. 5. My Sony headphones : a gift from my dad from one of his many business trips abroad. These headphones have accompanied me on every plane ride, workout and study session since. I am the student I am today because of noise-cancelling. Thank you, Dad. 6. Mentholatum Melty Cream Lip Balm : basically Japanese Aquaphor. 7. A banana clip : a hair accessory I recently discovered that has quickly become my favorite. It's not quite a claw clip, but it works perfectly with my thin hair. It lets me put my hair up and out of my face while I'm working without the headache-inducing tightness of a ponytail. 8. Blue-light glasses : spoiler alert: I have 20/20 vision, but I like wearing glasses, so it's me and my $12 blue-light glasses from Amazon against the world. After all, I need to protect my eyes somehow from the absurd amount of time I spend on GoodNotes every week. 9. Mini portable fan : the most recent addition to my bag. Baltimore's end-of-summer humidity has been a rude awakening for me. I'm never taking Cali weather for granted again. 10. An Omamori : a protective amulet from my senior trip to Tokyo. Knowing this little amulet is in my bag feels like I'm carrying a bit of good luck wherever I go. It reminds me to trust that everything will work out, even when I'm far from home and still figuring things out for myself. Reflecting on the long-term residents of my bag left me feeling oddly nostalgic and homesick and, in a way, gave me a better understanding of myself. I never really gave much thought to why I carry these things beyond what they're designed to do, but I've realized that each one has its own story and is, in some way, uniquely meaningful to me. Together, they represent the people, places and moments that have shaped who I am. Of course, I have been warned about using a shoulder bag for college, but I'll check back at the end of the semester, hopefully still with symmetrical shoulders and no back problems.

articles.title: SGA discusses sexual violence resources and reporting with OIE
articles.description: On Tuesday, Oct. 6 The 114th Student Government Association convened for their weekly general body meeting. This week's meeting began with a presentation from The Office of Institutional Equity (OIE) and Vice Provost Rachel Hernandez about sexual misconduct policies at Hopkins and reporting to OIE. She emphasized that the meeting would be one of several conversations with student organizations and leadership groups throughout the month. Representatives from the Office of Institutional Equity (OIE) outlined how the office receives reports and conducts intake and risk assessments. Reports can come directly from individuals, through responsible employees or through online submissions, including anonymous reports. Administrators spoke on how outreaches center on giving information about a survivor's options, confidential resources and supportive measures. Further, reporters or victims are not required to speak with OIE or press formal charges to get any form of desired assistance. Supportive measures mentioned by OIE in their presentation included academic accommodations, such as assignment extensions or excused absences, alongside adjustments intended to help students feel safer on campus. Following OIE's presentation, representatives from Public Safety and the Johns Hopkins Police Department spoke about their roles in supporting survivors of sexual crimes. They emphasized the importance of minimizing further trauma, protecting privacy and clarifying available options without pressuring individuals towards a certain path. Multiple attendees raised questions and concerns for administrators. One student asked whether recent news of alleged sexual misconduct at Cornell University would lead to changes in OIE's procedure for supporting victims and pursuing investigation in cases of sexual violence. Administrators responded that they always reflect on and update policies to reflect legal attitudes, lessons from other investigations and evolving student needs. A member of the public raised his hand to express frustration about the early mention of Blue Jay Safety Month before other resources in Friday's University broadcast message about sexual assault resources, stating that he felt the placement was dismissive of the reality of sexual violence. Vice Provost Hernandez explained that the month's programming included important prevention training and education while assuring the student that the placement was not meant to be facetious. Following the departure of the University administration from the room, the discussion between SGA concerning campus safety and prevention of sexual violence continued. Many members of SGA stated frustration at the fact that the measures taken by the University had failed to consider the issue of accountability and the culture among the students in Fraternity and Sorority Life (FSL) and Athletics. Secretary Honora Muratori argued that online prevention training is rarely taken seriously by students and is not effective in curbing sexual violence in college campuses. She urged SGA to advocate for in-person training, particularly for students in athletics or FSL. Civic Engagement Chair Jackson Morris encouraged senators to gather student feedback before returning to administrators. He further argued that SGA must ask difficult questions about cultural and organizational norms that promote sexual violence, such as hazing rituals and fraternity culture. Following this, there was a swearing-in ceremony of newly elected members of the Class of 2030 as well as an SGA Advisor. For cabinet reports, Student Body President Jason identified three objectives of the year: engagement, student experience and school spirit. Lastly, senators discussed funding bills related to nutrition education, sexual assault education and a photo shoot/networking event for Black students. Black Caucus Senator Oluwanifemi Ajayi proposed an initiative aiming to bring Black students together and launch an Instagram page to highlight the achievements of Black students, organizations and faculty at Hopkins. The SGA deferred the selection of the Senator of the Month for next week.

articles.title: Chernobyl particles reveal unexpectedly stable nuclear fuel after 40 years
articles.description: Four decades after the 1986 nuclear disaster, researchers at Leibniz University Hannover and the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) examined six tiny, highly radioactive fragments that were released from the destroyed reactor in Ukraine in the wake of the incident. Analyses show that these "hot particles" are far more stable than had previously been assumed. The findings could allow for more precise assessments of the health risks posed by such radioactive particles. The paper is published in the Journal of Hazardous Materials.

Hydrothermal vents supply a geochemical precursor of ATP that could have powered early life
articles.description: Where did the energy come from to power the chemical origin of life, and how did phosphate come to be the universal energy currency of cells? Biologists from the Institute of Molecular Evolution at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU) have uncovered a new source of energy that drove primordial chemical reactions on the early Earth forward to kick-start metabolism. Their findings, now published in The FEBS Journal, identify phosphite and palladium, substances that naturally occur in H2-producing hydrothermal vents, as an inorganic precursor of ATP.
